h1: Expectation bias and how a label changes what you taste
title: How a Label Changes What You Taste | Craft Beer School
desc: How expectation bias works in beer tasting: why price, style, brand and colour change what you taste and how blind tasting keeps you honest.
teaser: Tell people a beer is a rare import and it tastes better. Your brain does that before the beer reaches your tongue.
standfirst: What you expect to taste shapes what you do taste. A label, a price, a style name or a famous brewery can all push your judgement before the first sip. Knowing how it works is the first step to tasting fairly.
sections: Your brain tastes before your tongue does

Taste is not a simple reading from the tongue. The brain combines signals from taste, smell, sight, touch and memory, then adds what it expects. When the signals are faint or mixed, which they often are with beer, expectation fills the gaps.

That is expectation bias. It is not a lack of skill. Experienced tasters are affected too, sometimes more, because they hold firmer ideas about what a style or a brewery should taste like.

One of the best known demonstrations came from wine research in Bordeaux. A white wine was dyed red with a flavourless colouring and given to trained wine students. Many described it with the vocabulary of red wine, words such as red fruit and berry, rather than the terms they would use for white wine.

The students were not foolish. Colour set up an expectation. The brain then found flavours to match it. The same thing happens with beer every day. A dark beer gets described as roasty and heavy before anyone has checked whether it actually is.

Many cues change what people report:

  • Style name. Tell people a beer is an IPA and they look for hops and bitterness. Call the same beer a pale ale and they report less.
  • Brand and reputation. A famous brewery's beer gets the benefit of the doubt. A small unknown gets picked apart.
  • Price. A ₹600 bottle tends to be judged more kindly than a ₹150 one, even when the beer is similar.
  • Origin. An import from Belgium or Germany can taste more authentic simply because of the label.
  • Colour and clarity. Haze suggests fruit and softness. Dark colour suggests roast and body.

Our guide on reading a beer label covers what labels actually tell you, which is useful information. The trick is to read it after you taste, not before.
Why it matters beyond the pub

For a drinker, bias is mostly harmless. It may even add to the fun. For a brewer, it can be expensive. A panel that knows which tank a sample came from will often miss a fault in the beer it expects to be good. A head brewer who knows a recipe change was made will often find a difference that a blind panel cannot.

Bias also cuts the other way. If a team believes a new supplier's malt is inferior, they may taste problems that do not exist and reject a perfectly good batch. Neither error is visible unless you test blind.
How to strip the label away

The fix is blind tasting, done properly. Pour the beers out of sight. Use identical glasses filled to the same level. Code each sample with a random three digit number, not A, B and C or 1, 2 and 3, because people read meaning into letters and order. Serve samples in a different order to each taster where you can.

Where colour could give the game away, use black or dark glasses, or a dim red light. Our guide on tasting blind to strip colour bias covers that in detail.

Then ask tasters to write their notes before any discussion. The first person to say this one tastes of mango can plant mango in half the room.

Small breweries often run informal tastings where everyone knows what is in the glass. That is fine for enjoying beer and useless for quality control. A short daily panel with coded samples, even with only three tasters, gives far more honest results. Our guide to a ten minute daily taste panel shows how to run one without slowing production.

The person who prepares the samples should not taste them, or should taste last after writing down their own notes. It sounds fussy. It is the difference between a panel that finds faults and one that confirms what everyone already thought.

At your next tasting with friends, pour two similar beers into identical glasses while everyone looks away. Write a three digit code under each. Ask everyone to describe both and say which they prefer, then reveal. Watch how often the preferred beer is not the one people expected.
faqs: What is expectation bias in beer tasting?
It is when what you expect, from the label, price, brand or colour, changes what you actually taste. The brain fills gaps in faint signals with what it predicts.
How do you avoid bias when tasting beer?
Taste blind, with identical glasses, random three digit codes and the serving order changed for each taster. Write notes before anyone talks.
Are experienced tasters affected by bias?
Yes. Experience can make it stronger because experts hold firm ideas about what a style or brewery should taste like.
